version.changelog: AI-powered auto-repair system for OpenClaw with iflow integration

llm.summary: The skill claims to be a lightweight OpenClaw auto-repair helper but includes system-level install scripts, code that reads logs and can call external CLIs/services (iflow, webhooks), and installation advice that downloads/executes remote scripts — the footprint and behaviors are broader than the simple description and deserve careful review before installing.

dimensions.detail: The SKILL.md declares only python and openclaw as requirements and frames the skill as an OpenClaw 'self-healing' skill, but the package contains many executable components (install.sh/install.py, watchdog, openclaw_memory.py, iflow_bridge.py, notify.py) and docs that expect git, iflow CLI, sudo (creating /usr/local/bin symlinks, systemd/LaunchAgent/Task Scheduler templates), and even publishing tokens. Several required abilities (creating system services, modifying PATH, generating BAT files on the desktop, pushing to GitHub) are more invasive than the single-purpose description suggests.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions and docs instruct the agent and user to read OpenClaw logs/config (~/.openclaw paths), generate and save diagnostic and BAT files (potentially on the desktop), call the iflow CLI, and (in docs) push code to GitHub. While reading OpenClaw logs/config and restarting services is consistent with repair, generating executable BAT files for users, automatic invocation of an external AI CLI (iflow) and suggestions to upload/publish repository content expand the scope beyond simple repair and introduce data transmission and system modification steps that are not strictly limited to the stated purpose.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no formal install spec in the registry metadata, but the repository includes install scripts and README/INSTALL files that recommend 'openclaw skills install https://github.com/...' and even curl | bash from raw.githubusercontent.com. Those flows involve downloading and executing remote installer scripts (moderate-to-high risk). The included install scripts propose creating symlinks in /usr/local/bin and setting up LaunchAgent/systemd/Task Scheduler entries (requires elevated privileges).
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required environment variables, yet documentation and code reference external credentials and endpoints: CLAWDHUB_TOKEN for publishing, optional iflow CLI login (used to transmit diagnostics/repair records to 'iflow memory'), and optional notification webhooks (Feishu/DingTalk/Discord). The ability to collect logs/diagnostic reports and send them to iflow or webhooks means sensitive runtime data (logs, config, repair records) can be transmitted externally — this capability is not explicitly declared in requires.env and is material to user privacy/security.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always:true and is user-invocable. However, its install scripts and templates create long-lived system integrations (LaunchAgent, systemd unit, Task Scheduler entries, PATH changes, symlinks). These actions grant persistent presence and can run with elevated privileges if the user follows the provided install steps. Users should treat installer-run privileges as sensitive and audit the install scripts before granting.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
What to consider before installing

- Review the code first: this package is not instruction-only — it includes install scripts and Python modules (watchdog, notify, iflow_bridge, openclaw_memory) that will read OpenClaw logs/config and can create system services and files. Inspect install.sh, install.py, openclaw_memory.py, iflow_bridge.py and notify.py for network calls and what files they read/write.

- Network/data exfiltration risk: the skill can use the iflow CLI and configurable webhooks to send diagnostic data and repair records off your machine. If you have sensitive logs or secrets in OpenClaw config, consider disabling 'iflow' features and webhook notifications in config.json (enable_iflow_helper / iflow_memory / alert settings) before enabling auto_heal.

- Avoid piping remote scripts into shell: README suggests curl | bash from raw GitHub. Instead, download the repository, inspect the installer locally, and run install steps manually. Do not run installers as root unless you understand and trust every operation.

- Limit privileges and test in safe environment: run in a VM or disposable test environment first. Start with auto_heal=false, disable BAT generation (enable_bat_generation=false) and notifications, run diagnose/--dry-run to see what actions would be taken.

- Audit persistent changes: if you proceed, check any created systemd/LaunchAgent/task scheduler entries, PATH modifications, and symlinks. Remove them if you decide to uninstall.

- If unsure, consider 'suspicious' indicators: the skill's documentation includes publishing/pushing guidance and tokens (CLAWDHUB_TOKEN) unrelated to runtime repair; that's development/publishing guidance and not required for repair — be cautious about following publishing instructions on a production machine.

What would increase our confidence one way or the other

- If the maintainer provided an explicit install spec (trusted release tarball or package manager entry) and clarified which network calls are made and exactly what data is sent to iflow/webhooks, that would reduce concern.
- If the skill documented a clear opt-in flow for transmitting diagnostics (and defaults to OFF), and the install scripts avoided system-wide changes or required elevated permissions only after explicit consent, the assessment could move toward benign.
